title: When 1.5 million balloons fell – C1 English Reading Test

seo.title: When 1.5 million balloons fell – C1 English Reading Test - Test-English
seo.description: Take a C1 English reading test about an event gone wrong in Cleveland, with seven reading comprehension questions and detailed feedback.

parts:
C1 English Reading Test

Read the text about an unusual record-breaking event. For questions 1–7, choose the correct answer (A, B, C or D).

When 1.5 million balloons fell

At 1:50 p.m. on 27 September 1986, the sky above Cleveland appeared to vanish. A vast net opened in Public Square, releasing a cloud of helium balloons that swallowed buildings, wrapped itself around Terminal Tower and briefly turned a grey afternoon into a scene from a children’s film. Below, more than 100,000 spectators cheered. For the organisers, everything seemed to be going exactly to plan. It was not.

Balloonfest ’86 had been devised by the charity United Way with a view to raising money and giving Cleveland some positive publicity. Thousands of volunteers had spent hours inflating balloons beneath an enormous mesh roof. The original target was two million. Faced with an approaching storm, however, the organisers treated the warning not as a reason to cancel but as a reason to bring the release forward. They stopped at 1,429,643 balloons—still enough to break Disneyland’s world record.

At first, the balloons behaved as expected. They rose together, and the organisers believed they had created a spectacle for which the city would long be remembered. They could not have been more right. Normally, helium balloons rise, disperse, and eventually descend as their pressure drops. These encountered cool air and rain almost immediately. Instead of dispersing, many remained inflated and were pushed back towards the ground. Within minutes, the celebratory cloud had become something drivers, pilots and rescue workers had to deal with.

Balloons landed on roads and waterways, contributing to traffic accidents as motorists tried to avoid them. At Burke Lakefront Airport, a runway was temporarily closed. Thousands more settled on Lake Erie, where their bright colours made objects in the water difficult to distinguish from one another. On top of that, balloons frightened valuable Arabian horses, prompting their owner to sue over alleged lasting injuries. Others travelled much farther; weeks later, they were reportedly washing up on the Canadian side of the lake. None of these incidents was disastrous in isolation. Together, however, they transformed a publicity triumph into a growing liability.

The most serious controversy concerned two fishermen who had disappeared during severe weather the previous night. The Coast Guard found their empty boat and began searching the lake. Crew members said the balloons covering the surface made the operation more difficult, since a floating head or life jacket could easily be mistaken for one of them. The men’s bodies were later recovered, and the wife of one fisherman brought a lawsuit that was settled privately.

This grim detail has frequently been simplified online into the claim that Balloonfest killed the men. The evidence does not support such a definite conclusion. A Coast Guard search specialist interviewed decades later argued that the fishermen would probably have died before the balloons were released and that the event had not caused their deaths. The balloons complicated the search; whether that changed its outcome is another matter.

At the time, Balloonfest was hailed as a record-breaking achievement. Today, it is more often held up as a lesson in unintended consequences. The release of the balloons gave rise to lawsuits and environmental damage; whether it also contributed to two deaths is far less certain. The uncertainty surrounding that link may make for a less dramatic internet story, but the truth is extraordinary enough without presenting an unproven claim as fact.

Questions

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the text?

choices.html: To give a balanced account of a notorious event.
To assign responsibility for a public disaster.
To investigate the failure of a rescue operation.
To condemn a publicity-driven charity campaign.

questions.prompt: What can be inferred about the organisers' response to the approaching storm?

choices.html: They didn't think the storm would influence the success of the event.
They inflated fewer balloons to cut the preparations short and get ahead of the storm.
They had been expecting poor conditions throughout the preparations.
They considered setting the record more important than public safety.

questions.prompt: What does the writer imply by saying, 'They could not have been more right'?

choices.html: The organisers had predicted how the weather would affect the event.
The event proved even more spectacular than the organisers had anticipated.
Cleveland became famous for its record-breaking achievement.
The event was remembered for the wrong reasons.

questions.prompt: Why does the writer describe how helium balloons normally behave?

choices.html: To show that the organisers used the balloons incorrectly.
To argue that nobody could have predicted the outcome of the release.
To contrast their expected dispersal with their sudden return to the ground.
To explain how some of the balloons eventually reached Canada.

questions.prompt: What does the writer mean by saying that the incidents transformed 'a publicity triumph into a growing liability'?

choices.html: The publicity became increasingly difficult to control as news spread beyond Cleveland.
An apparent success gradually became a source of problems and potential costs.
The organisers' achievement was overshadowed by the magnitude of the storm.
Each new incident caused more serious damage than the one before it.

questions.prompt: Which statement best reflects the writer's conclusion about Balloonfest and the fishermen's deaths?

choices.html: The balloons probably prevented the Coast Guard from finding the fishermen in time.
The private settlement showed that the organisers accepted responsibility for the deaths.
The balloons hindered the search, but their effect on its outcome cannot be established.
The later expert evidence proved that the original rescue crews had been mistaken.

questions.prompt: What concern does the writer express about some internet accounts of Balloonfest?

choices.html: They may favour drama over factual accuracy.
They ignore how the event was perceived at the time.
They give too much attention to its legal and environmental effects.
They fail to report how extraordinary the event was.
